pass1.sentence: First-aid guidance describes back blows and abdominal thrusts for severe choking, 999 if the blockage stays, and a medical check after abdominal thrusts.
pass1.note: Search text: back blows then abdominal thrusts; 999 if not relieved; assessment by a healthcare practitioner after abdominal thrusts.

pass1.sentence: Mild choking is described as being able to speak, cough or breathe, and encouraging the person to keep coughing is the advice.
pass1.note: Red Cross: mild = can speak, cough or breathe; encourage coughing.

pass1.sentence: Severe choking is described as being unable to speak, cough or breathe, and the person may become unconscious without help.
pass1.note: Red Cross: severe signs and eventual unconsciousness.

pass1.sentence: For adults, first-aid sources describe up to five back blows, then up to five abdominal thrusts, repeated in turn.
pass1.note: NHS inform and Resus Council: back blows then abdominal thrusts, alternated.

pass1.sentence: Babies under one are described as having back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.
pass1.note: NHS baby page: five back blows then five chest thrusts; NEAS: no abdominal thrusts under one.

pass1.sentence: Anyone treated with abdominal thrusts is described as needing a check by a health professional afterwards.
pass1.note: 111 Wales and Resus Council: assessment after abdominal thrusts because of possible injury.

pass1.sentence: First-aid guidance describes mild choking as a person who can still speak, cough or breathe.
pass1.note: Red Cross: mild signs.

pass1.sentence: Such a person can usually clear the blockage alone, and the advice is to encourage them to keep coughing.
pass1.note: Red Cross: encourage coughing.

pass1.sentence: The British Red Cross also mentions asking the person to spit out the object if it is in the mouth.
pass1.note: Red Cross adult page via search summary: ask to spit out the object.

pass1.sentence: Fingers are not put into the mouth when the object cannot be seen.
pass1.note: Red Cross: do not put fingers in mouth if object cannot be seen.

pass1.sentence: Severe choking is described as being unable to speak, cough or breathe.
pass1.note: Red Cross: severe signs.

pass1.sentence: Without help, the person eventually becomes unconscious.
pass1.note: Red Cross: becomes unconscious.

pass1.sentence: For a child, the British Red Cross adds that they may be clutching at the chest or neck.
pass1.note: Red Cross child page: may clutch chest or neck.

pass1.sentence: NHS inform describes giving up to five sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand.
pass1.note: NHS inform: back blows, up to 5, heel of hand between shoulder blades.

pass1.sentence: If the blockage remains, it describes abdominal thrusts, with a fist placed between the navel and the bottom of the breastbone and pulled sharply inwards and upwards.
pass1.note: NHS inform: abdominal thrusts description.

pass1.sentence: The Resuscitation Council UK 2025 guidance describes up to five back blows, then up to five abdominal thrusts, and then alternating the two.
pass1.note: Resus Council 2025 first aid guidelines: up to 5 back blows then up to 5 abdominal thrusts; alternate 5 and 5.

pass1.sentence: The alternating continues until the blockage clears or the person becomes unresponsive.
pass1.note: Resus Council: until relieved or unresponsive.

pass1.sentence: The Red Cross describes the abdominal thrusts as a step for people who are trained.
pass1.note: Red Cross via search summary: abdominal thrusts 'if trained'.

pass1.sentence: The Resuscitation Council UK advises against blind finger sweeps of the mouth.
pass1.note: Resus Council: do not use blind finger sweeps.

pass1.sentence: NHS-linked guidance says abdominal thrusts are not used on babies under one year old or on pregnant women.
pass1.note: Search text, NEAS cited for this caution; pregnancy part attributed to the search summary of NEAS/NHS-linked pages.

pass1.sentence: NHS 111 Wales says that if the airway is still blocked after back blows and abdominal thrusts, 999 is called and the operator is told the person is choking.
pass1.note: 111 Wales: call 999 if still blocked after both.

pass1.sentence: The Resuscitation Council UK describes calling 999 if choking has not been relieved after five abdominal thrusts.
pass1.note: Resus Council 2025: call 999 if not relieved after five abdominal thrusts.

pass1.sentence: St John Ambulance describes calling 999 or 112 straight away if the blockage has not cleared.
pass1.note: SJA adult page via search summary.

pass1.sentence: The wording on timing differs a little between sources, but each links the call to a blockage that has not cleared.
pass1.note: Synthesis of the three statements above.

pass1.sentence: If the person becomes unresponsive, the Resuscitation Council UK describes starting CPR and making sure 999 has been called.
pass1.note: Resus Council: start CPR and ensure 999 called.

pass1.sentence: The British Red Cross describes opening the airway by lifting the chin and tilting the head, then checking breathing.
pass1.note: Red Cross: open airway, check breathing.

pass1.sentence: If the person is not breathing, it describes CPR, pressing straight down 5 to 6 cm on the chest using body weight until an ambulance arrives.
pass1.note: Red Cross: CPR compressions 5-6cm until ambulance arrives.

pass1.sentence: The NHS describes up to five sharp back blows, with the baby lying face down along the thigh or forearm.
pass1.note: NHS baby page: up to five back blows, face down on thigh or forearm.

pass1.sentence: If the blockage stays, the NHS describes up to five chest thrusts, with the baby face up and two fingers on the breastbone.
pass1.note: NHS baby page: up to five chest thrusts, two fingers on breastbone.

pass1.sentence: Abdominal thrusts are not used on babies under one.
pass1.note: NEAS: do not use abdominal thrusts under one.

pass1.sentence: North East Ambulance Service describes calling 999 if the blockage is not dislodged.
pass1.note: NEAS via search summary: call 999 if not dislodged.

pass1.sentence: The Resuscitation Council UK paediatric algorithm likewise alternates five back blows with five chest thrusts for an infant.
pass1.note: Resus Council paediatric algorithm 2025 via search summary: infant, alternate 5 back blows, 5 chest thrusts.

pass1.sentence: St John Ambulance mentions that a baby who has had chest thrusts should still be seen in hospital, even if the blockage clears.
pass1.note: SJA baby page via search summary.

pass1.sentence: The NHS pairs back blows with abdominal thrusts for children over one.
pass1.note: NHS child page: back blows plus abdominal thrusts.

pass1.sentence: It describes a clenched fist above the navel and below the ribs, pulled sharply inwards and upwards, repeated up to five times.
pass1.note: NHS page: fist above navel, below ribs, up to five times.

pass1.sentence: The British Red Cross says the force of the back blows depends on the size of the child, with much gentler blows for a smaller child.
pass1.note: Red Cross child page: change force by size.

pass1.sentence: It describes calling 999 if the blockage does not dislodge, and continuing back blows and abdominal thrusts until it clears, help arrives or the child becomes unresponsive.
pass1.note: Red Cross child page: call 999; continue cycles.

pass1.sentence: St John Ambulance describes checking the mouth after each blow or thrust, and starting child CPR if the child becomes unresponsive and needs it.
pass1.note: SJA child page via search summary.

pass1.sentence: NHS 111 Wales says a health professional, such as a GP or a doctor in A&E, should always examine someone after abdominal thrusts.
pass1.note: 111 Wales: always examine after abdominal thrusts.

pass1.sentence: The Resuscitation Council UK gives the reason that complications and injuries can occur after abdominal thrusts or chest compressions.
pass1.note: Resus Council: evaluated by healthcare practitioner since complications and injuries may occur.

pass1.sentence: St John Ambulance says the same for children who received abdominal thrusts, even if the blockage has cleared.
pass1.note: SJA child page via search summary.

pass1.sentence: NHS 111 Wales also advises urgent medical help if a persistent cough follows or if the person feels something is still stuck in the throat.
pass1.note: 111 Wales via search summary.

pass1.sentence: The Resuscitation Council UK published new guidelines in 2025, so its current pages are the reference if details change.
pass1.note: Resus Council 2025 guidelines; search says implementation in courses from January 2026.
